extracted.intended_audience: students/readers learning algebraic topology (undergraduate/early graduate), users of Evan Chen's 'Napkin' notes
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and computational tools for singular and cellular homology and cohomology: long exact sequences, relative homology, excision, cellular homology and boundary formulas, degrees of maps, and the universal coefficient theorem. Includes definitions, key theorems, examples, and computation recipes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Splitting of short exact sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: An exact sequence which splits lets us obtain B given A and C. In particular, (b) holds anytime C is free. The short exact sequence 0 → Z → eH1(X) → Z → 0 therefore splits when C = Z or any free abelian group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When C is free abelian (for example Z), condition (b) in the splitting lemma is necessarily true and the short exact sequence splits, giving B ≅ A ⊕ C. Counterexamples (non-splitting) include sequences like 0 → Z/2Z → Z/4Z ↠ Z/2Z which do not split because Z/4Z ≇ Z/2Z ⊕ Z/2Z. The splitting lemma is valid in any abelian category; 'direct sum' is the appropriate colimit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-splitting example (Z/4Z)
rubrics_metrics.description: The short exact sequence 0 → Z/2Z → Z/4Z ↠ Z/2Z → 0 does not split because Z/4Z is not isomorphic to Z/2Z ⊕ Z/2Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such concrete finite abelian group examples to test splitting: even when two end-terms are isomorphic to Z/2Z, the middle term's structure matters. This is an anti-pattern to assuming splitting without checking module structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long exact sequence of a pair
rubrics_metrics.description: For a subspace A ⊆ X, there is a long exact sequence ··· → Hn(A) → Hn(X) → Hn(X,A) → Hn−1(A) → ··· and a reduced version ··· → eHn(A) → eHn(X) → Hn(X,A) → eHn−1(A) → ···.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence to compute relative and absolute homology groups by breaking spaces into simpler pieces. The triple long exact sequence also holds: ··· → Hn(B,A) → Hn(X,A) → Hn(X,B) → Hn−1(B,A) → ··· for A ⊆ B ⊆ X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative homology = quotient space (when hypotheses satisfied)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a space and A is a closed subspace such that A is a deformation retract of some open set V ⊆ X, then the quotient map q : X → X/A induces an isomorphism Hn(X, A) ≅ Hn(X/A, A/A) ≅ eHn(X/A). (Theorem 73.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem gives the main criterion for when relative homology coincides with homology of the quotient: A must be closed and a deformation retract of an open neighborhood. Counterexamples occur when A is not closed or these hypotheses fail (see earlier examples). Use excision and deformation retraction in the proof and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excision theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Z ⊆ A ⊆ X be subspaces such that the closure of Z is contained in the interior of A. Then the inclusion ι : (X \ Z, A \ Z) → (X, A) induces an isomorphism Hn(X \ Z, A \ Z) ≅ Hn(X, A). (Theorem 73.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excision allows deleting a subset Z of A when computing Hn(X,A) provided closure(Z) ⊂ interior(A). Intuitively, modding out A makes internal points of A irrelevant, but one must check the topological hypothesis (closure in interior) to avoid cutting cycles apart (counterexamples exist). Practical use: reduce complicated pairs to simpler ones by excising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative homology for contractible subsets
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a topological space and A ⊆ X is contractible, then for all n, Hn(X,A) ≅ eHn(X). (Lemma 73.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since eHn(A)=0 for contractible A, the long exact sequence segment 0 → eHn(X) → Hn(X,A) → 0 is exact, giving the isomorphism. In particular applies when A is a point; uses contractibility as a sufficient condition for this simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative homology generalizes absolute homology
rubrics_metrics.description: For any space X and point * ∈ X, Hn(X,{*}) ≅ eHn(X); and Hn(X, ∅) = Hn(X). (Lemma 73.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are base cases that relate relative homology to the ordinary (absolute/reduced) homology; use them when converting between relative and absolute computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category of pairs and functoriality
rubrics_metrics.description: A map of pairs f : (X,A) → (Y,B) is a map f : X → Y with f(img(A)) ⊆ B. Pair-homotopy is homotopy through maps of pairs. There is a functor Hn : hPairTop → Grp; pair-homotopic maps induce the same map on relative homology. (Lemma 73.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pair-homotopy equivalences to replace pairs by simpler ones (deformation retracts) when computing relative homology. Functoriality ensures induced maps behave well under composition and homotopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformation retract of a pair
rubrics_metrics.description: A ⊆ X is a deformation retract of X if there is a map of pairs r : (X,A) → (A,A) which is a pair-homotopy equivalence. In this situation Hn(X,A) ≅ Hn(A,A) = 0. (Definition 73.3.6 and Example 73.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical examples: a point being a deformation retract ⇒ X contractible; Dn \ {0} deformation retracts onto Sn−1; Rn \ {0} retracts onto Sn−1. If A is a deformation retract of an open neighborhood V, use excision and the quotient to relate Hn(X,A) to Hn(X/A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology of wedge sums
rubrics_metrics.description: If X and Y are spaces with basepoints x0 ∈ X, y0 ∈ Y and each basepoint is a deformation retract of some open neighborhood, then for every n we have eHn(X ∨ Y) = eHn(X) ⊕ eHn(Y). (Theorem 73.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Theorem 73.4.3 to the disjoint union X ⨿ Y with the subset {x0,y0} and collapse to form the wedge; ensures homology of wedge is direct sum of reduced homologies when basepoints are suitably nice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local homology groups and invariance of dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The k-th local homology group at a point p in X is Hk(X, X \ {p}). Excision shows this depends only on a neighborhood of p. For Rn, Hk(Rn, Rn \ {x}) ≅ Z if k = n and 0 otherwise. Using local homology, if U ⊂ Rn and V ⊂ Rm are nonempty open sets that are homeomorphic, then n = m. (Definition 73.6.1 and Theorem 73.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute local homology via excision to show dimension is a topological invariant for Euclidean open sets (Brouwer invariance of domain/invariance of dimension). Use local homology as a diagnostic for manifold dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of a map Sn → Sn
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n > 0 and map f : Sn → Sn, f* : Hn(Sn) ≅ Z → Hn(Sn) ≅ Z is multiplication by an integer d; this integer is the degree deg f. (Section 74.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: deg(f ∘ g) = deg(f) deg(g); maps homotopic have equal degree; reflection has degree −1; antipodal map has degree (−1)^{n+1}. Intuition: degree counts algebraic covering number ('how many times f wraps Sn around itself'). Hopf's theorem: equal degrees imply maps are homotopic on Sn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hairy ball theorem (application of degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n > 0 is even, then Sn does not have a continuous field of nonzero tangent vectors. (Theorem 74.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: constructing a nonvanishing tangent field would produce a homotopy between id and −id on Sn, forcing deg(id)=deg(−id)= (−1)^{n+1}, contradiction when n is even. Use degree arguments to obstruct certain maps or structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cells_k(X) and cellular homology groups
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X, define Cellsk(X) = Hk(X^k, X^{k−1}). Then Hk(X^k, X^{k−1}) ≅ Z^{(# of k-cells)} when k equals the index, and zero otherwise; furthermore Hk(X^n) stabilizes to Hk(X) for n large. (Lemma 74.2.1 and Definition 74.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cells_k(X) is a free abelian group with basis the k-cells. Use the skeleton filtration and long exact sequences to compute these groups and to assemble the cellular chain complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular chain complex and d_k differentials
rubrics_metrics.description: The cellular chain complex is ... → Cells_{k+1}(X) d_{k+1}→ Cells_k(X) d_k→ Cells_{k−1}(X) → ... with d_{k}∘d_{k+1}=0; the kth homology of this complex is isomorphic to Hk(X). (Theorem 74.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the cellular chain complex from the long exact sequences of the skeleton pairs (X^n, X^{n−1}). This yields a much smaller, computationally tractable chain complex than singular chains for CW complexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cellular boundary formula (k>1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ek be a k-cell and {e_{k−1}^β} the (k−1)-cells. Then d_k(ek) = Σ_β d_β e_{k−1}^β where d_β is the degree of the composed map Sk−1 = ∂ek (attaching map) → X^{k−1} ↠ Sk−1_β (the quotient collapsing X^{k−1}\e_{k−1}^β). (Theorem 74.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute each coefficient by composing the attaching map with the quotient collapsing away other (k−1)-cells and taking the degree. This counts multiplicity and orientation contributions (e.g., explains multiplicity 2 in Klein bottle). For k=1, d1 is the usual difference of endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm for computing homology via cellular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: (1) Cells_k(X) = Z^{#k-cells}. (2) d1: Cells1→Cells0 is boundary map (difference of endpoints). (3) For k>1, for each k-cell compute degrees d_β to get dk(ek)=Σ d_β e_{k−1}^β. (4) Compute homology as ker(d_k)/im(d_{k+1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to explicit CW decompositions (torus, Klein bottle, projective spaces, complex projective spaces). Keep track of orientations and edge identifications to compute degrees; watch for identifications that reverse orientation producing torsion factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples: torus and Klein bottle cellular homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Torus built with one 0-cell, two 1-cells a,b and one 2-cell attached by aba^{-1}b^{-1} gives cellular differentials d1=d2=0 and H_*(T^2)=Z, Z^2, Z. For the Klein bottle with attaching word abab^{-1}, d2(e2)=2 e1_a, giving H1(K) ≅ Z ⊕ Z/2Z and H2(K)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These worked examples illustrate how attaching maps determine dk and can produce torsion (the factor 2 for Klein bottle). Use these as templates when analyzing other CW complexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic via Betti numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: For any finite CW complex X, χ(X)=Σ_n (−1)^n · #(n-cells of X) and equals Σ_n (−1)^n rank Hn(X). (Theorem 74.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses ranks in exact sequences for skeleton filtrations. Use Betti numbers (bn = rank Hn(X)) to compute Euler characteristic independent of CW decomposition. Practical check: compute both cell-count formula and Betti-number formula for sanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology: cochain complex and singular cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: A cochain complex A^• is dual to a chain complex; H^n(A^•) = ker(δ: A^n→A^{n+1}) / im(δ: A^{n−1}→A^n). For a space X and abelian group G, the singular cochain complex is C^*(X;G)=Hom(C_*(X),G) and H^n(X;G)=H^n(C^*(X;G)). (Definitions 75.1.1 and 75.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 0-cochains are functions X→G and H^0(X;G) corresponds to functions constant on path components. Cohomology groups often carry extra structure (G-module, ring structure) when G is a ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: For every n, H^n(−;G) is a contravariant functor from hTop^op to Grp: maps f : X→Y induce f^* : H^n(Y;G) → H^n(X;G); pair-homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology. (Theorem 75.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functoriality is obtained by dualizing the singular chain functor and using chain-homotopies (prism operator) to show homotopic maps induce equal maps on cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal coefficient theorem for cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A_• be a chain complex of free abelian groups and G an abelian group. There is a natural short exact sequence 0 → Ext(H_{n−1}(A_•), G) → H^n(A_•;G) → Hom(H_n(A_•), G) → 0, and this sequence splits, so H^n(C_•;G) ≅ Ext(H_{n−1}(C_•),G) ⊕ Hom(H_n(C_•),G). (Theorem 75.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem shows cohomology is determined (up to Ext contributions) by homology. For computations over Z and many spaces, compute Hom and Ext of the homology groups to obtain cohomology. Be mindful of torsion: Ext captures torsion contributions to cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of H^0(X;G)
rubrics_metrics.description: C0(X;G) consists of all functions X → G, and H^0(X;G) is the subgroup of such functions constant on path-connected components, so H^0(X;G) ≅ G^r when X has r path-connected components (finite case). (Example 75.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For infinite component sets, cohomology and homology differ (direct product vs direct sum phenomena). Use this to check base-level computations and to understand differences between H_0 and H^0.
